claims.text: Adding a small amount of an oxygen-affinitive element such as Hf to Co-free FeNiCrMn can improve its strength-ductility balance under dynamic loading.
The proposed intervention is applicable from room temperature to 800°C.
The proposed intervention is applicable at strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
Adding Hf or another oxygen-affinitive element will form a stable oxide dispersion in FeNiCrMn.
The stable oxide dispersion will improve strength.
The stable oxide dispersion will improve ductility.
Stable oxides formed by oxygen-affinitive additions can act as strengthening precipitates.
The oxide precipitates will increase the alloy's resistance to deformation.
The modified alloy may have greater yield strength than unmodified FeNiCrMn.
The modified alloy may have greater ultimate tensile strength than unmodified FeNiCrMn.
The modified alloy may have greater toughness than unmodified FeNiCrMn.
The initial material may be either as-cast or wrought Co-free FeNiCrMn.
The comparator is as-cast or wrought Co-free FeNiCrMn without an added oxygen-affinitive element.
The exact type and amount of oxygen-affinitive addition and the optimal processing conditions remain uncertain.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing modified and unmodified FeNiCrMn through tensile testing and microstructural analysis over multiple temperatures and strain rates.
Failure to improve the strength-ductility balance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is framed specifically around dynamic loading, but the stated range extends down to 10^-3 s^-1, which is ordinarily a quasi-static rather than dynamic strain rate.
